title: Beanie Babies: Reigning Toy Craze Champion
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the Beanie Babies craze of the 1990s, the reigning toy bubble. They cover Ty Warner's background and firing from his sales job, the 1993 launch of Beanie Babies at five dollars, the retailer-only distribution and retirement-based scarcity tactics, the 1995 website and early e-commerce sales, the 1997 and 1998 McDonald's Happy Meal promotions, the secondary market and eBay boom, price guides by Mary Beth Sobaluski and Peggy Gallagher, odd crime and divorce stories, the 1999 end-of-line announcement and Christmas Eve vote, the eventual crash, comparisons to bitcoin, Warner's later tax case and hotel ownership, and the 2023 movie The Beanie Bubble. The episode also includes a live-show tour announcement and a sponsor-style break; listener mail was skipped.

segments.title: Tour announcement teaser
segments.summary: Hosts tease upcoming 2024 live shows in Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco at SketchFest and urge listeners to buy tickets from official sellers.

segments.title: Festive opening and classic toy tradition
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as the pre-Christmas classic toy episode and note they have done toy episodes before.

segments.title: Introduction to the Beanie Baby bubble
segments.summary: The hosts describe Beanie Babies as one of the biggest market bubbles, with most buyers being adults who believed the toys would gain value.

segments.title: Ty Warner's early life and firing
segments.summary: Ty Warner's childhood in the Chicago suburbs, his Kalamazoo College theater background, his flamboyant salesman persona, and his 1980 firing for using company time and lists to sell his own products.

segments.title: Origins: plush cats and the Beanie Baby launch
segments.summary: After living in Rome, Warner made named plush cats before launching Beanie Babies in 1993 at about five dollars, with bead stuffing, birthdays, and poems on heart tags.

segments.title: Retailer-only distribution and scarcity
segments.summary: Beanie Babies were sold only through licensed retailers such as gift and hospital shops, in limited allocations, which created a sense of scarcity and collecting.

segments.title: Internet website and early e-commerce
segments.summary: An employee, Lena Trevetti, pushed for a Beanie Babies website in 1994 and sales began online in 1995, and the movie The Beanie Bubble is discussed as loosely based on Zach Bissonette's book.

segments.title: Secrecy, retirements, and manufactured scarcity
segments.summary: Warner kept production secret and retired models without warning, such as Chocolate Moose, which drove collectors and retailers to stockpile.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode sponsor break.

segments.title: McDonald's Teenie Beanies promotion
segments.summary: The 1997 and 1998 McDonald's Happy Meal promotions with Teenie Beanies produced record sales, purchase limits, and people chasing the toys.

segments.title: Beanies as investment and the eBay secondary market
segments.summary: Adults treated Beanie Babies as an alternative investment, and about six percent of eBay sales in 1997 were Beanie Babies; retired toys sold for high prices.

segments.title: Price guides and the people who profited
segments.summary: Peggy Gallagher's self-published book and Mary Beth Sobaluski's price guide and magazine made money, and Sobaluski's Chicago-area trading helped start the national trend; the HBO documentary Beating Mania is mentioned.

segments.title: Vegas divorce and the Beanie Baby pick-up
segments.summary: A 1999 Las Vegas divorce case where a judge had the couple divide their beanie babies, and the wife's objection to the process.

segments.title: Chris Robinson Senior and the Bankrupt by Beanies documentary
segments.summary: A California man spent about one hundred thousand dollars on twenty thousand Beanie Babies, and his son made the short documentary Bankrupt by Beanies.

segments.title: Beanie Baby crime stories
segments.summary: Counterfeiting and fake sales, theft of Beanie Babies including the Beanie Baby Bandit Ben Perry, and the Jeffrey White killing of Harry Simmons in West Virginia.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode sponsor break.

segments.title: Bubble bursts: 1999 end announcement and Christmas Eve vote
segments.summary: Warner announced in August 1999 the end of production, then reversed on Christmas Eve with a fifty-cent vote for charity, and ninety-one percent voted to continue.

segments.title: Decline and Princess Diana bear glut
segments.summary: Sales spiked briefly, the craze lasted until about 2002, and the Princess Diana and Claude bears were overproduced, leaving collectors' stockpiles nearly worthless.

segments.title: Comparison to bitcoin and speculative bubbles
segments.summary: The hosts compare the Beanie Baby bubble to cryptocurrency and bitcoin, advising against holding bubble assets long term.

segments.title: Ty Warner's wealth, Four Seasons, and tax case
segments.summary: Warner's Forbes net worth, his Four Seasons New York hotel dispute, his charitable donations, and his tax evasion sentence over a Swiss account.

segments.title: Later products, licensing, and the movie
segments.summary: Licensing deals with Garfield and Disney, Beanie Booze, Warner's continued marketing, and his comments about who should have played him in The Beanie Bubble.

segments.title: Fake eBay listings and gift card scams
segments.summary: Inflated secondary-market listings and gift card payment demands are flagged as likely scams.

segments.title: Listener mail skipped and tour reminder
segments.summary: Listener mail is skipped this week; hosts remind listeners about the Pacific Northwest tour and ticket scams.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck gives contact email and closes the episode.
